extracted.intended_audience: journalists, editors, newsroom leaders, and media researchers interested in news judgment and source bias
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance/synthesis about how publication source and platform affect journalists' judgments of newsworthiness, based on a survey of U.S. newspaper journalists. Useful for people assessing or studying how stories are selected or valued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source prestige influences perceived newsworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Publication source (prestige) affects how newsworthy journalists rate a story, even when content is held constant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey results show that stories published in national or mid-sized newspapers were judged about the same as unpublished items, while stories published in local newspapers were rated as less newsworthy. Evaluators should be aware that identical content can be valued differently simply because of where it appeared.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local stigma / devaluation of local-appeared stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that have appeared in local outlets are systematically devalued in newsworthiness judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study labels this as a 'local stigma' — publication in a local outlet reduces perceived newsworthiness even controlling for content. This implies a bias against sourcing or republishing items that originated in local journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social-media provenance (Twitter) as a newsworthiness signal
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence on Twitter — including anonymous, context-free tweets — can be judged as newsworthy by some journalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inexperienced journalists and heavy Twitter users in the survey rated anonymous, context-free tweets as about as newsworthy as AP headlines. Thus, social-media exposure or virality can substitute for traditional source signals for some evaluators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextlessness does not necessarily disqualify
rubrics_metrics.description: Lack of context (e.g., short or anonymous tweets) does not automatically make an item un-newsworthy for some journalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The finding that context-free tweets were rated as newsworthy indicates that verification, background, and context may be undervalued in social-media-driven news judgments. Editors should consider policies to counteract contextlessness being treated as sufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credibility and objectivity can be decoupled from newsworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: For some journalists, newsworthiness is disconnected from other news values such as credibility and objectivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The survey suggests a 'profound disconnect between newsworthiness and other significant news values' — meaning an item can be judged newsworthy despite low credibility or lack of verification. This is a caution against equating perceived newsworthiness with factual reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluator characteristics (experience and platform use) shape criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: A journalist's experience level and use of Twitter affect how they apply newsworthiness criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inexperienced journalists and heavy Twitter users were more likely to rate minimal social-media items as newsworthy. Assessment frameworks should account for heterogeneity among evaluators and consider training or editorial guidelines to reduce such variance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness is socially constructed
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsworthiness is not an intrinsic property of content but is shaped socially by who evaluates it and by what signals (like source prestige) they use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the same content can be judged differently depending on prior publication venue, news organizations and researchers should treat 'newsworthiness' as contingent and subject to bias rather than as a fixed quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithmic distribution may amplify source-based biases
rubrics_metrics.description: Algorithms that distribute stories can magnify existing biases in perceived newsworthiness tied to source prestige.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The implication is that automated systems could further undervalue local journalism or boost items with advantageous source signals. Designers and editors should consider how algorithms weight provenance and engagement signals to avoid reinforcing unfair devaluations.
